meta.title: AutoGen/AG2 and Multi-agent Patterns
meta.thesis: AutoGen/AG2 and Multi-agent Patterns is practical when learners can apply it to this concrete case: A research workflow uses planner, researcher, writer, and critic agents to produce a migration brief. By the end, they should be able to build or review AutoGen-style role and handoff protocol, measure reviewer catches missing evidence before final answer, and catch the failure where agents talk endlessly because no one owns termination.

mentalMap.caption: Teach AutoGen/AG2 as conversation-based multi-agent orchestration with user proxies, tools, termination, and version caveats.
mentalMap.oneLineThesis: AutoGen and AG2 are useful when the lesson is about agents talking, delegating, using tools, and stopping through conversation protocols.

modules.title: Conversation is the orchestration surface
modules.sub: Agents coordinate by messages rather than graph edges.
modules.summary: AutoGen/AG2 makes agent collaboration look like structured conversation.
objectives: Explain user proxy and assistant roles.
Name the risk of open-ended chats.

blocks.title: AutoGen-style agents negotiate through messages

spans.text: Problem anchor: a data analyst agent writes a query, a code executor runs it, and a human user proxy approves the final chart before it is shared. The interesting part is not just tool calling; it is who speaks next and when the conversation ends.
AutoGen and AG2 belong to the conversational-agent family. Agents exchange messages, request tools, ask humans, and stop when a termination rule or workflow condition fires.
If the task does not need conversation among participants, a simpler chain or graph may be clearer.

blocks.analogy: AutoGen is closer to a moderated meeting than a conveyor belt.

blocks.title: Case study: analyst, executor, and user proxy

spans.text: The analyst proposes SQL, the executor runs it in a sandbox, and the user proxy approves the externally shared summary. Each participant has a bounded role.
The conversation ends when the analyst sends a final answer that passes an evidence check and the user proxy approves sharing.

items.text: Register tools only with the executor that needs them.

blocks.title: Conversation fit
blocks.prompt: What makes AutoGen/AG2 distinctive for this lesson?

options.text: It is only a vector database.
Agents coordinate through message exchange, tools, user proxies, and termination rules.
It removes the need for human approval.

blocks.explanation: The core abstraction is conversational orchestration.

modules.title: Conversable agents need roles, tools, and termination
modules.sub: A team is safe only when each participant has boundaries.
modules.summary: The team contract lives in agent roles and termination logic.
objectives: Assign tools to the right agent.
Define max turns and final markers.

blocks.title: Every participant needs an exit condition

spans.text: AG2-style `ConversableAgent` patterns are powerful because any participant can reply, call tools, or hand work to another participant. That also means the system needs clear termination: max turns, keywords, evaluator pass, approval, or explicit state.
Tools should be assigned by responsibility. A reviewer does not need code execution; a user proxy does not need broad database credentials.
Write the phrase that ends the conversation and the condition that makes it valid.

blocks.analogy: A group chat without a stop rule becomes a meeting with no agenda.

cells.text: Breaks task down and proposes next work.
Runs code or tools in sandbox.
Unsafe code if sandbox is weak.

blocks.title: Termination rule
blocks.prompt: Why is max-turn or final-marker logic important?

options.text: It lets every tool run without validation.
It prevents unbounded conversations and makes completion testable.
It hides all intermediate messages.

blocks.explanation: Conversational teams need explicit stopping conditions.

modules.title: Version names and AG2 continuity matter
modules.sub: AutoGen examples can point to different APIs.
modules.summary: AutoGen, AgentChat, Core, AG2, and Microsoft Agent Framework are not interchangeable.
objectives: Identify AutoGen maintenance and AG2 continuity caveats.

blocks.title: The name changed faster than the concept

spans.text: Microsoft AutoGen has multiple eras, and AG2 continues the classic AutoGen lineage. Microsoft also points new production agent work toward Microsoft Agent Framework. A lesson should say which family it is teaching.
Do not mix AutoGen 0.2 snippets, current stable AutoGen AgentChat, AG2 docs, and Agent Framework workflows without explanation. Learners will install the wrong package or follow the wrong API shape.
Include the package, docs family, and date on every practical example.

blocks.analogy: Framework names are street signs; follow the one on the current map.

blocks.title: Worked version note for a lesson

spans.text: A lesson that says “AG2-style ConversableAgent” should link to AG2 docs and explain the relation to older AutoGen. A Microsoft production lesson should instead point to Microsoft Agent Framework.
This avoids sending greenfield learners toward a maintenance-mode path when the subject is not legacy AutoGen literacy.

items.text: Choose AutoGen AgentChat, AutoGen Core, AG2, or Microsoft Agent Framework.
State what the example is not covering.
Run a smoke test after dependency updates.

blocks.title: Version caution
blocks.prompt: Why should a lesson date-stamp AutoGen/AG2 claims?

options.text: Dates make tool schemas invalid.
Tutorials and APIs span different framework generations and can conflict.
AG2 has no documentation.

blocks.explanation: Version clarity prevents learners from copying incompatible examples.

modules.title: Code execution belongs in a sandboxed participant
modules.sub: The executor role is a security boundary when designed correctly.
modules.summary: A multi-agent chat still needs runtime policy.
objectives: Route tool execution through a bounded executor.

blocks.title: Tool authority should not leak across the chat

spans.text: If a planner can both invent code and run it with full filesystem access, the “team” has no safety separation. Put execution behind a participant with sandbox limits, allowed tools, and structured results.
Spaced recall: from agent safety, tool output is untrusted. The planner may read executor output, but policy still controls follow-up side effects.
The final answer should cite executor output or human approval, not only chat confidence.

blocks.title: Tiny conversation loop with final marker
blocks.explanation: The toy loop makes speaker ownership and termination visible; a real AG2/AutoGen app would use framework agents and sandboxed executors.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Before reading the answer, predict whether the reviewer sends FINAL.
predictThenReveal.answer: The reviewer sends FINAL because the executor message includes evidence.

blocks.title: Executor boundary
blocks.prompt: Which participant should usually own code execution?

options.text: Every participant equally.
A bounded executor with sandbox and tool policy.
The final reviewer with no logs.

blocks.explanation: Execution is authority and should be scoped.

modules.title: Evaluate conversation traces, not only final text
modules.sub: Multi-agent chat can look smart while hiding duplicated or unsupported work.
objectives: Check human approval and sandbox use.

blocks.title: The trace is the product evidence

spans.text: A healthy AutoGen/AG2 trace shows each participant doing its job, tools running under the right participant, evidence flowing into the final answer, and termination happening for the intended reason.
Failure modes include runaway chats, repeated planning, executor overreach, unsupported final claims, weak user-proxy approval, and version drift after package updates.
Compare the conversation team against a single-agent or deterministic baseline on the same task.
Read the final answer with the conversation trace open.

items.text: Each participant had a distinct role, allowed tools, and stop rule.
Code or browser execution happened only in sandboxed executor roles.
The user proxy approved exact artifacts or actions, not vague intent.
The final answer cites evidence produced or verified in the conversation.
Turn count, cost, and failures beat or justify a simpler baseline.

blocks.title: Trace review
blocks.prompt: What should block release of a conversational agent team?

options.text: A trace that includes useful evidence.
A final answer that relies on unsupported worker claims or unauthorized tool execution.
A clear termination marker.

blocks.explanation: Conversation style does not exempt the system from grounding and safety checks.

framework.label: Framework
framework.laymanDefinition: A library or platform that provides agent building blocks and conventions.
framework.technicalNote: Framework choice affects state handling, tools, tracing, deployment model, ecosystem fit, and how much control the application keeps.

graph.label: Graph
graph.laymanDefinition: A workflow shape where nodes and edges define how work moves between steps.
graph.technicalNote: Graph-based agents make branching, retries, checkpoints, and human review more explicit than a single loose loop.

checkpoint.label: Checkpoint
checkpoint.laymanDefinition: A saved workflow state that lets execution resume or be inspected later.
checkpoint.technicalNote: Checkpoints are essential for durable agents because retries, approvals, and debugging need the exact state at a step boundary.

handoff.label: Handoff
handoff.laymanDefinition: Passing work from one agent, tool, or human role to another.
handoff.technicalNote: Handoffs need a typed payload, ownership transfer, stop condition, and audit trail so context does not vanish between actors.

sdk.label: SDK
sdk.laymanDefinition: A software development kit with APIs and helpers for building applications.
sdk.technicalNote: Agent SDKs encode assumptions about models, tools, sessions, tracing, and deployment, so evaluate those assumptions against the product architecture.

orchestration.label: Orchestration
orchestration.laymanDefinition: Coordinating steps, agents, tools, state, and decisions in a workflow.
orchestration.technicalNote: Orchestration owns sequencing, parallelism, retries, timeouts, approvals, and failure visibility across the agent system.

finalCheck.title: Knowledge check
finalCheck.intro: A quick check across the whole lesson — pick or type your answers.

questions.prompt: In AutoGen/AG2's conversation-based orchestration model, what is the PRIMARY role of the UserProxyAgent?

options.text: Generate LLM responses and propose tool calls on behalf of the user
Act as the human-side participant that triggers turns, enforces termination, and optionally executes code
Host the vector database that grounds the assistant's replies
Broadcast messages to all agents simultaneously via a pub/sub bus

questions.explanation: The UserProxyAgent represents the human side of the conversation: it initiates turns, can run code, and decides when to stop — the AssistantAgent handles LLM reasoning.

questions.prompt: You are setting up a two-agent chat and want it to stop automatically without human intervention. Which combination correctly enforces termination?

options.text: Set max_turns on the chat and include a recognized termination string (e.g., 'TERMINATE') in the assistant's final message
Set temperature=0 on the LLM config so the model always produces the same output
Assign all tools to the UserProxyAgent so it can decide when no tools remain
Use a GroupChat with a single speaker_selection_method='round_robin' and no max_round

questions.explanation: AutoGen/AG2 terminates a chat when max_turns is reached OR when the configured termination marker (default 'TERMINATE') appears in a message — both guards are needed for reliable auto-stop.

questions.prompt: A colleague points you to the 'AutoGen' GitHub org maintained by Microsoft for a new greenfield project. What is the key caveat you should raise?

options.text: Microsoft's repo uses a different programming language and is not Python-compatible
The Microsoft-maintained 'AutoGen' repo diverged from the original; the community continuation is AG2 (ag2ai), and mixing docs between the two families causes API mismatches
Microsoft deprecated AutoGen entirely and replaced it with Semantic Kernel, so neither repo should be used
Both repos are identical forks and either set of docs is safe to follow interchangeably

questions.explanation: After the fork, Microsoft's AutoGen and the community's AG2 (ag2ai) diverged in API and roadmap — using docs from the wrong family leads to import errors and missing features.

questions.prompt: Why should code execution be routed through a sandboxed participant (e.g., a Docker-based executor) rather than run directly in the orchestrating process? Name at least TWO distinct reasons.
questions.acceptableAnswer: Acceptable answers should include at least two of: (1) isolation — a sandbox prevents malicious or buggy generated code from harming the host system or leaking secrets; (2) reproducibility / clean environment — each execution starts from a known state; (3) evidence capture — stdout/stderr from the sandbox is recorded as a message in the conversation trace, making it auditable; (4) role boundary enforcement — keeping execution out of the orchestrator preserves clear agent responsibilities and makes termination markers predictable.
questions.explanation: Sandboxing protects the host from unsafe generated code AND produces a structured execution record that becomes part of the auditable conversation trace.

questions.prompt: When evaluating a completed multi-agent run, which of the following is the MOST complete evaluation strategy?

options.text: Read only the final assistant message and check whether it answers the original question
Inspect per-agent message logs, verify tool calls and sandbox outputs, count turns against budget, confirm human-approval steps fired, and check total token cost
Re-run the conversation with temperature=0 and compare outputs for determinism
Check that no Python exceptions were raised during the run

questions.explanation: Evaluating only the final answer misses hidden failures; a full trace review covers tool correctness, cost, turn efficiency, sandbox use, and human-in-the-loop compliance.
